video_title: The Bond Market Is Trapping The Fed | Weekly Roundup
gist: Two Blockworks hosts, recording the day after a firm PPI print and the day before CPI, argue that Bessent's $6 billion long-end buyback was called by the bond market — yields rose anyway — with a nominal-GDP regression implying 10-year fair value near 5.8% versus a market being held roughly 100bp below it. They frame the Fed as facing a fork with two bad paths into a $100 oil shock, handicap a September hike (odds moved to ~70%), and argue a term-premium-driven 'credibility hike' would actually pull long-end yields down, while the debasement trade stays intact but path-risky and the levered semiconductor/AI trade needs six to twelve months of healing.

themes.theme: Treasury buybacks versus the bond market

insights.claim: Bessent escalated long-end Treasury buybacks from the traditional $2 billion to a $6 billion announcement — above his own $4 billion minimum guidance — and the long end still sold off with yields higher, which the hosts read as the bond market calling his bluff and demanding roughly double the ammunition.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: The size threshold matters: if the next buyback escalation is not dramatically larger, the intervention has been proven ineffective and long-end yields have room to keep rising.
insights.quote: the market saying that look, $6 billion dollars of buybacks is not enough if you're trying to fight us. Um, you got to at least double that thing, buddy.

insights.claim: A regression of the 10-year against nominal GDP puts fair value near 5.8% on roughly 6.6% nominal GDP, meaning the administration is attempting to hold at least a 100 basis point spread below fair value through intervention.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete anchor for how far the long end could travel if intervention fails or nominal GDP stays hot — a ~100bp gap to close.
insights.quote: the fair value of the 10-year is somewhere around 5.8% right now roughly speaking

insights.claim: The yen leg of the intervention has quietly worked where the bond leg has not — formal intervention began in the 160s and the pair is now at 153, helped by a more hawkish Bank of Japan.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Intervention efficacy is asset-specific: currency intervention is holding while bond-market intervention is failing, which argues against treating 'the trade is manipulated' as a blanket thesis.
insights.quote: the yen has worked out, honestly, which is, you know, I feel like it's kind of gone understated

insights.claim: Bessent's behaviour is best modelled as rational political incentive rather than ideology — he built his reputation at Soros breaking the Bank of England and would be on the other side of this trade if he were outside government, but with midterms a month and a half away he has to balance suppressing yields and weakening the currency against the inflation those actions create.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Positioning should assume intervention persists until the midterms and then loses its political sponsor — the incentive clock, not the rhetoric, is the trade.
insights.quote: he's not the devil and he's not the Lord. Like he's he's just another, you know, politician and policy maker trying to keep the ball afloat

themes.theme: The Fed's fork with two bad paths

insights.claim: Central banks hiking into an energy supply shock has many historical precedents across Europe and the US and the hikes are typically reversed within twelve months, because rate hikes do not create more oil and in fact restrict production by raising financing costs.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: If the Fed hikes into $100 oil, position for the reversal rather than the cycle — historically the hike is unwound inside a year and sows a recession.
insights.quote: central bank hikes don't create more oil

insights.claim: The other path is equally bad: weakening the dollar, stimulating commodities, suppressing bond yields and intervening to support asset prices all inject demand into a supply shock, which is the COVID-style inflation mechanism — the correct policy is to sit still and let the supply side resolve.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Frames both policy branches as inflationary or recessionary — the direct implication is that real assets and inflation hedges keep working across both paths.
insights.quote: you don't want to be stimulating demand into a supply shock otherwise you get COVID crazy levels of inflation

insights.claim: That a hike is even on the table is the direct consequence of the administration's own stimulus — the SPR, bond market and currency interventions, and tariff refunds — rather than of organic economic strength.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: The policy mix is self-defeating: fiscal and market intervention is generating the inflation that forces the monetary tightening it was designed to avoid.

insights.claim: The right policy would be to stop hiking on the front end and let the long end find fair value, but political incentives prevent it because the housing market has ground to a halt and financing conditions are already very restrictive for longer-tail small businesses and consumers.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Watch housing and small-business credit as the constraint that eventually forces the Fed to choose inflation over restriction.
insights.quote: ultimately they will pick inflation, but again these paths on the way there get get really dicey because neither are very good

insights.claim: Odds of a September hike have moved to roughly 70% (versus 30% for a pause) after the PPI print, up from about 50/50 a week earlier, with Waller's stated reaction function making tomorrow's CPI single-handedly decisive.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: A single data print now controls a binary policy outcome — an unusually clean event-risk setup for options around the CPI release and the FOMC.
insights.quote: we're down to about a 30% odds of a pause and and about 70% odds of a hike

insights.claim: Waller's dogmatic pre-commitment — publicly stating he will vote to hike if CPI comes in above consensus and otherwise will not — is criticised as excessive, with the hosts noting he may be salty about not receiving the chair appointment.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Pre-announced reaction functions make the Fed's decision mechanically forecastable from the data, which raises the market's sensitivity to individual prints.

insights.claim: The likeliest outcome is framed as a reluctant insurance or credibility hike sold as one-and-done, given both Trump appointees like Waller who are publicly at odds with the chair and anti-Trump committee members who would welcome a hike into the election.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: The composition of committee politics, not the data alone, is pushing toward a hike — and a one-and-done framing has very different asset implications than the start of a cycle.

insights.claim: The SOFR curve has three hikes priced into June and September of next year, which is judged very hard to exceed — ripping three hikes into $120 oil would mean an absolute beating for equities and a recession — so the curve is a fade, but only once the hiking actually starts.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: A specific fade trade with an explicit trigger condition: wait for the first hike before selling the front end, because kicking the can can reflexively price even more.
insights.quote: if they did three if they ripped three hikes in the next six to nine months like you got to imagine the stock market's taking an absolute beating

themes.theme: Long-end composition and the credibility-hike trade

insights.claim: Historical analysis of long-bond behaviour around first hikes shows the composition of the yield rise matters: when inflation expectations lead, long yields keep rising through the hike, but when term premium is the driver — as it is now — a one-and-done credibility hike is followed by long-bond yields falling.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: The actionable version: if CPI forces a hike framed as insurance rather than the start of a cycle, receive the long end rather than selling it.
insights.quote: when it's term premier le, you know, that's really the bond market screaming for we need a credibility hike

insights.claim: The curve has flattened hard into this episode and structural problems remain at the long end, so the cleaner expression may be SOFR rather than the long bond — with steepening likely on the other side if the Fed turns dovish on growth and no longer needs to cap the long end.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Flags a steepener as the sequel trade once growth problems replace inflation as the Fed's binding constraint.

insights.claim: As the 10-year approaches 5%, it is reaching the upper bound of what underlying real growth plus inflation should command — with equities only now beginning to care about a signal the bond market has been sending for some time.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: The equity-versus-bond divergence closing is the risk event; equities repricing to a 5% 10-year is the mechanism for the next drawdown.
insights.quote: the bond market's been saying this and and equities are only starting to care now that it's in the purview

insights.claim: August PPI was hot on headline while core came in at 0.2% month-over-month, slightly below the 0.3% consensus, with PPI services soft except transport and warehousing — a gas-price pass-through story visible in breaking-out wholesale diesel — and the PCE-relevant components benign, portfolio services at -1.6% being the clearest example.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance), citing Guy LeBas
insights.so_what: The print is neutral on substance but is being traded as hot; the real signal is energy pass-through, which will keep feeding through as oil holds $100.
insights.quote: overall a neutral reading with a hint of energy price pass through and an easy easy push into PCE

insights.claim: Judging prints against consensus obscures the level problem: printing a 4-handle month-over-month toward almost 5% year-over-year is structurally problematic regardless of whether it came in line, and the benign PCE components — portfolio services — are irrelevant to the roughly 80% of people who own no portfolio.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: A framework warning against in-line-print complacency: zoom out to the level and trend, which is re-accelerating, rather than the surprise versus consensus.
insights.quote: when expectations point 4% month over month and you're printing, you know, with the four handle into the almost fives year-over-year, like it's still super problematic

insights.claim: The base case is that inflation comes in firm with risk skewed to the upside, with little disinflation further out and a possible total revamp higher over coming months given what oil is doing — making it very difficult for the Fed not to hike over coming meetings.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Position for upside inflation surprises rather than the disinflation path still embedded in much of the curve.
insights.quote: it should not surprise anyone if in the next year or two there's four, five, six inflation

insights.claim: The sticky drivers of inflation — notably wage growth — are still not accelerating, which is the stated reason for not endorsing a sustained hiking cycle; the current impulse is oil, headline and its derivatives.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Gives the specific indicator that would flip the call from one-and-done to a genuine hiking cycle: wages turning and accelerating.

themes.theme: Growth, AI capex and the post-midterm air pocket

insights.claim: Growth is judged to be peaking because its two main drivers — fiscal deficit spending and AI investment — are decelerating in rate of change, while lagged real rates above 2% work through, junk spreads on the longer end widen, and financial conditions outside equities tighten.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Positions for a growth downshift into next year even without a recession call, with widening junk spreads as the early confirmation signal to watch.
insights.quote: Spreads on the long uh like junkier stuff are widening.

insights.claim: The post-election outlook is unattractive regardless of the result: the pre-midterm fiscal impulse falls away and is replaced by debt-ceiling and budget fights, congressional gridlock, and political backlash against data centers — with Democrats expected to take the House and possibly the Senate.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: The fiscal impulse supporting markets has a known expiry date; historically the compromises that follow are more spending and less market-friendly, which is inflationary.

insights.claim: Hostility to AI and data centers has become bipartisan, with candidates who previously supported data centers flipping to anti-data-center positions because polling has moved so aggressively — and frontier-lab executives tweeting doomsday and job-loss scenarios are actively damaging their own permitting and political position.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Political risk is becoming a real constraint on the data-center buildout that underpins both the AI trade and a large share of GDP growth — watch state-level permitting and campaign positioning.
insights.quote: it's a bipartisan hatred of AI right now

insights.claim: The AI industry is repeating 2021 crypto: wealth created from nowhere mints young people into unprecedented money and power, producing a cloak of invincibility and hubris that gets tested — and even a Republican Senate hold costs enough political capital to reduce the administration's ability to run coercion tactics with corporations, foreign governments and supply chains.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: A framework for why political support for the AI buildout is more fragile than the market assumes, drawn from a directly analogous cycle the hosts lived through.
insights.quote: the the cloak of invincibility that seems to be kind of draped over the industry is it's going to get tested like it every one of these frontier tech industries do

themes.theme: Debasement trade and the levered momentum unwind

insights.claim: The debasement trade's narrative got ahead of itself on the buyback announcement, but the thesis is unchanged into next year — the discipline is refusing to be stopped out during a murky pre-FOMC drawdown when the entry price provided enough P&L buffer to absorb it.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Entry price is what buys the ability to hold through path risk; the stated plan is to give back short-term gains rather than risk being right on thesis and stopped out.
insights.quote: the last thing I want to do right now personally is end up being right on my thesis but getting stopped out in the interim

insights.claim: Part of the policy game is deliberately letting air out and letting volatility expand to ding the debasement trade in order to run the next leg, so holders must expect engineered drawdowns rather than a straight line — and the dips are to be bought.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Explains the trade's chop as intentional rather than thesis-invalidating, and argues for hedging with equity beta while holding the core position.
insights.quote: part of the game is that they also need to let air out and let V expand and basically you know kind of ding the the debasement trade in order to to kind of run the next leg

insights.claim: Sustaining Nvidia at a five-and-a-half to six trillion dollar market cap against a multi-trillion bond market will require increasingly large government interventions, while inflation at three and a half percent coexists with a potential growth problem.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: Frames the mega-cap AI complex as dependent on continued policy support, tying its valuation directly to the intervention regime rather than to fundamentals.

insights.claim: Once a trade becomes levered to the gills — hundreds of billions in 3x levered ETF volume, a fund running $40 billion at four times leverage — and then rinses out, that area should be avoided for a minimum of six months and possibly a year, because relief rallies drag in trapped top buyers.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: A concrete time-based rule for avoiding the semiconductor complex after a leverage unwind, independent of whether the price low is already in.
insights.quote: once that stuff gets to the main page and then rinses out, that's usually an area you don't want to go near for a minimum six months, maybe a year

insights.claim: The bottom in the semiconductor unwind may already be in — called the day after Leopold was liquidated out of the trade — but that does not make it a good trade; it is dead money while the built-up leverage works through, the same pattern seen in bitcoin and in gold and silver after January.
insights.speaker: host (Blockworks, Forward Guidance)
insights.so_what: Separates price-bottom from opportunity-cost: post-unwind assets range for months, so capital is better deployed in the emerging leadership.
insights.quote: I think bottoms in, but it doesn't mean it's a good trade. Like, it's going to be dead money for a while.

insights.claim: Oil positioning remains surprisingly light relative to a deteriorating supply-demand picture, a worsening situation in Iran and a vertical price line — investors keep returning to the trades they know instead of recognising the new leadership that has emerged.
insights.speaker: Quinn, co-host
insights.so_what: The clearest fresh long in the episode: energy leadership with positioning still not crowded, versus crowded and rinsed-out metals and semis.
insights.quote: the oil positioning uh data is still fairly light for what I'd expect it to be
